acceptable.choice: Spring Boot (Spring MVC, Java 21+ with virtual threads) with JDBC or JPA, a small HikariCP pool, and the existing Postgres
acceptable.why: It is the stack the three developers already know and can review, and about 200 small inserts a second is a modest load that a single tuned Spring Boot instance can handle within 1 vCPU / 512 MB.

acceptable.choice: Spring Boot tuned for the small VM: -Xmx around 200–300 MB or MaxRAMPercentage, SerialGC, capped thread and connection pools, lazy init and only the starters it needs
acceptable.why: The JVM's default settings are what make Java look memory-hungry; with explicit limits the service fits safely in 512 MB.

acceptable.choice: Plain JDBC (JdbcTemplate or jOOQ) with batched inserts and a simple index on parcel ID for status lookups
acceptable.why: It keeps write cost and memory low and stays easy for reviewers to read.

acceptable.choice: Spring Boot built as a GraalVM native image (Spring AOT), as an optional optimisation
acceptable.why: It cuts memory use and startup time, but adds build complexity and reflection quirks. Use it only if measurement shows the JVM version doesn't fit.

acceptable.choice: Quarkus or Micronaut on Java, as a secondary option
acceptable.why: Same language and a smaller footprint, but a new framework for a three-person team. Only justified if tuned Spring Boot fails a load test on the real VM.

acceptable.choice: Spring WebFlux / R2DBC, acceptable but not preferred
acceptable.why: It works within the resource limits, but reactive code is harder to review and debug than MVC with virtual threads, and this load doesn't need it.

ruled_out.choice: Go, Rust, Node.js, Python, Elixir or another non-Java back end
ruled_out.why: Nobody in IT can review or maintain it, which breaks the 'IT can keep everything running' and 'review every change' requirements; any resource saving isn't needed at this load.

ruled_out.choice: Kafka, RabbitMQ or another message broker in front of the database
ruled_out.why: It won't fit comfortably on a 512 MB VM, adds infrastructure three people must run, and 200 writes a second doesn't need it.

ruled_out.choice: Kubernetes or another container orchestration platform
ruled_out.why: Too much operational overhead for three developers, and a poor match for the standard small VMs at a local host.

ruled_out.choice: Public-cloud managed or serverless services (AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, Firebase, etc.)
ruled_out.why: Company policy says it runs on VMs at the local hosting company.

ruled_out.choice: Switching the database to NoSQL or a time-series store (MongoDB, Cassandra, InfluxDB)
ruled_out.why: It adds a new system to operate and new skills to learn; Postgres handles this write rate easily.

ruled_out.choice: Adding Redis or another cache layer from the start
ruled_out.why: Another component to run and keep consistent, with no evidence yet that status reads need it.

ruled_out.choice: Untuned Spring Boot with default JVM settings and a heavy dependency set
ruled_out.why: It risks running out of memory or swapping on a 512 MB VM.

must_mention: Recommend staying with Java and Spring Boot because the team's skills and review responsibility outweigh small performance gains elsewhere.
About 200 small writes a second is modest for one tuned Spring Boot instance and for Postgres; no exotic technology is needed.
Give explicit memory tuning for 512 MB: heap cap or MaxRAMPercentage, SerialGC on 1 vCPU, bounded thread and connection pools, lean dependencies.
Load-test on an actual 1 vCPU / 512 MB VM at peak rate and above before going live.
Scan ingestion must be idempotent (client-generated scan ID plus a unique constraint), because handheld scanners retry on poor connections.
For reliability, run at least two instances behind the hosting company's load balancer or a reverse proxy, with health checks.
Plan Postgres sizing and growth: scan history grows by millions of rows a day, so add indexes for status lookups and a retention or partitioning plan.
Keep the code conventional and boring (Spring MVC, JDBC or JPA, Flyway migrations, standard actuator metrics) so three Java developers can review changes written by the agent.
red_flags: Recommending Go, Rust, Node or another language the team can't review, justified by performance or memory.
Claiming Java or Spring Boot can't run in 512 MB, or that the VM policy must change, without measuring.
Adding Kafka, Redis, Kubernetes, microservice splits or other infrastructure the team would have to run.
Suggesting cloud or serverless hosting despite the local-hosting policy.
Ignoring duplicate or retried scans, offline buffering on the scanners, or data loss when the single VM restarts.
Making reactive programming (WebFlux) or native image mandatory, which adds complexity the load doesn't call for.
Ignoring the database side (connection limits, indexes, table growth) while focusing only on the API process.
Giving no way to verify the choice, such as a load test on the real VM size.
unknowns: Where Postgres runs and how big it is: shared with other services or on its own VM, and its connection limits and disk speed.
How many status queries customers make at peak, and whether they come through a public website (which affects security and caching).
How long the high peak lasts, the total scans per day, and how long scan history must be kept.
Whether the scanners buffer and retry when offline, and what payload, protocol and authentication they use.
Whether the host provides a load balancer or allows several VMs for this service, and how VM failures are handled.
Which Java version and Spring Boot version the company has standardised on (virtual threads need Java 21+).
Latency and availability targets (SLA) for scan acceptance and status lookups.
Whether a tuned JVM actually stays within 512 MB under peak load, which only a load test on the real VM can show.
